draft.title: The two-sector circular flow model
card: The two-sector circular flow model has two sectors: households and businesses. Households own resources, such as labour, land and capital. They sell these resources to businesses.
Businesses pay households income for these resources, such as wages for labour, rent for land and interest or profit for capital.
Households then spend that income on the goods and services that businesses sell.
That spending becomes money for businesses, which they use to pay for resources again. So money flows around the economy in a circle.
draft.remember: In the two-sector model, households earn income from businesses for their resources, then spend it back on businesses.

a.q: Sam works at a cafe in Bendigo and spends his wages on a bike from a local shop. What does this show about money?
opts: It flows from business to household and back to business
It flows from household to business and then stops
It moves only between households and never to businesses
It is spent once and does not return to any business
a.why: The cafe pays wages to Sam, and he spends them at the bike shop, so money moves from business to household and back to a business. It does not stop, because the bike shop can pay for its own resources.
a.clue: Follow the money from the cafe to Sam to the bike shop.

b.q: A large factory in Geelong closes and its workers lose their jobs. What is a likely effect on local shops?
opts: Less income for households, so less spending at shops
More income for households, so more spending at shops
No change, as households do not spend their income
Shops gain money because workers stop selling labour
b.why: Without wages, households have less income to spend, so local shops are likely to sell less. Workers no longer selling labour means less income, not more.
b.clue: What happens to spending when wages stop?

a.best: It flows from business to household and back to business

b.best: Less income for households, so less spending at shops

problems.detail: The card lists only labour, land and capital, and pays 'interest or profit for capital'. Victorian textbooks usually use four factors of production: land earns rent, labour earns wages, capital earns interest, and enterprise earns profit. Tying profit to capital and leaving out enterprise could mislead students.

This question asks about the knock-on effect of job losses on shop sales. That is the idea of point 4 (how the sectors depend on each other). The card does not teach what happens when the flow is disrupted.

check.summary: Both questions have one clear right answer. The card pairs profit with capital instead of enterprise, and question b tests the chain-reaction idea that belongs to point 4.

proposal.title: The two-sector circular flow model
card: The two-sector circular flow model has two sectors: households and businesses. Households own the resources businesses need to make goods and services. These are called factors of production.
There are four factors. Land is natural resources. Labour is people's work. Capital is equipment, machines and buildings. Enterprise is the skill and risk of starting and running a business.
Businesses pay households income for each factor: rent for land, wages for labour, interest for capital and profit for enterprise.
Households spend that income on goods and services from businesses. Businesses use this money to pay for resources again, so money flows in a loop.
proposal.remember: Households earn rent, wages, interest and profit from businesses, then spend that income back at businesses.

a.q: Sam works at a café in Bendigo and spends his wages on a bike from a local shop. What does this show about money?
opts: It flows from business to household and back to business
It flows from household to business and then stops
It moves only between households and never to businesses
It is spent once and does not return to any business
a.why: The café pays wages to Sam, and he spends them at the bike shop, so money moves from a business to a household and back to a business. It does not stop there, because the bike shop uses that money to pay for resources again.
a.clue: Follow the money from the café to Sam to the bike shop.

b.q: Mei came up with the idea for a bakery in Ballarat and took the risk of starting it. What does the model say she earns for this?
opts: Profit, the income paid for enterprise
Wages, the income paid for labour
Rent, the income paid for land
Interest, the income paid for capital
b.why: Having the idea and taking the risk of starting a business is enterprise, and the income for enterprise is profit. Wages are tempting because Mei may also work in the bakery, but wages pay for labour, not for the risk of starting a business.
b.clue: Which factor is about the skill and risk of starting a business?

A second arrow from Households to Businesses is labelled 'Spending', and a second arrow from Businesses to Households is labelled 'Goods and services'.
wants.why: Seeing the arrows go both ways helps students picture money flowing around in a loop.
